title: The harvest that isn't only yours
hookLine: the first order covers blessings and farming
carry: a harvest is never only yours
last: IT ALL BELONGS TO ONE TORAH.

lines: A FIELD AT DAWN, READY TO CUT.
NAMED FOR WHAT GOES IN THE GROUND.
cards: A farmer walks out at dawn to a field of wheat that's ready. Before a single stalk is cut, a list of questions is waiting for her. Which edge of the field stays standing?
What happens to the stalks she drops? Did she plant two kinds of seed in one row? Is this the year the land is supposed to rest?
Which part goes to someone else? On a grocery receipt, a harvest looks simple. The Mishnah's first order sees a web of obligations, and it's named for what goes into the ground.

teach.b: Zeraim. Seeds. The first of the six orders opens with blessings, which is tomorrow's story, then goes out to the farm and stays there.
Walk a growing season with it.

teach.h: MIXED KINDS AND THE SEVENTH YEAR.
teach.b: Before planting, there's Kilayim, mixed kinds. The Torah says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt not sow thy field with two kinds of seed."
So the Mishnah asks the practical questions: how far apart must two crops be? What counts as two kinds? Then Sheviit, the seventh year.
The Torah tells the farmer to let the land rest, and says the poor may eat what grows on its own. Then the harvest, and here the gifts begin. Peah, the corner of the field, left for the poor.
Terumot and Maaserot, the portions set aside for the priests and the Levites, who had no fields of their own.

teach.h: THE CORNER, THE TITHES, FIRST FRUITS.
teach.b: And at the end of the order, Bikkurim, the first fruits brought up to the Temple. Notice the pattern. At every stage, the harvest is never only the farmer's.

teach.h: THE POOR, THE PRIEST, THE LAND, GOD.
teach.b: Something goes to the poor, something to the priest and the Levite, something to the land itself, which gets its rest, and something back to God.

teach.h: A HARVEST IS NEVER ONLY YOURS.
teach.b: Jewish law ties these farm laws largely to the land of Israel, so a Jewish farmer in Ohio isn't bound by most of them. But the order still speaks to anyone who eats: food arrives already carrying other people's shares.

how: Jews say a blessing before eating, with different endings for bread, fruit of the tree, fruit of the ground and other foods; in the land of Israel, farmers who keep these laws still set aside tithes and observe the seventh year.

o: the Torah's laws about which foods are kosher
the first fruits brought up to the Temple
seeds: the Mishnah's order on blessings and farming

s: Zeraim is only about how to grow crops well
it's about obligations: what's left for the poor, set aside for priests and Levites, and given back to God.
the Torah says the poor may eat what grows in the seventh year
the land rests, and what grows on its own is open to them.
the order of seeds opens with planting instructions
it opens with blessings. that's tomorrow's story.

games.q: you're a farmer in ancient Israel. the seventh year arrives. your field is good and your family could use the crop. what does the Torah tell you to do?
o: plant as usual and give some away.
let the land rest, and let the poor eat what grows.
games.why: the land rests, and what grows on its own is open to the poor. the Mishnah's tractate Sheviit works out how.

practice: Hold something small you're about to eat, an apple, a piece of bread, and trace it backward: who picked it, packed it, drove it, what field it grew in, what rain fell on it.
Before you eat, if you pray, you can say the blessing your tradition uses for that food. If you don't, name where it grew and one person who helped it reach you.
